title: The Moment Classroom Behavior Always Gets Worse
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin pinpoints a specific, teacher-controlled moment that reliably precedes a decline in classroom behavior: when a teacher states an expectation but fails to ensure it is actually followed, such as explaining how to ready laptops and then letting poor execution slide. He argues this single lapse is uniquely damaging because it teaches students that the teacher's words are mere suggestions, which erodes trust across every other area, including instruction, and gets generalized by students as something close to lying. Once this pattern repeats, students stop taking the teacher seriously and dismiss even the most basic directions. The concrete corrective he offers is that everything a teacher says must be backed by demonstrative action -- nothing can be allowed to slide -- which may require enforcing consequences, reteaching and redoing routines, or tightening freedoms such as dismissing students only a few at a time until expectations are met.
points: The decisive moment isn't a dramatic blowup -- it's the quiet failure to enforce a stated expectation, like ignoring poorly executed laptop routines.
Students equate a teacher's unenforced words with lying, which taints their trust in everything else the teacher says, including academic instruction.
Corrective action can include reteaching a routine, tightening freedoms, or dismissing students only a few at a time until they meet the standard.
Standing firm on small expectations, once believed impossible with a given group, is what causes students to eventually regard the teacher as a leader worth listening to.
quotes: It’s when the teacher verbalizes an expectation, but doesn’t ensure that it’s followed. A simple example would be explaining to students how you want them to take out and ready their laptops, but then ignoring its poor execution.

This is so profoundly detrimental because it communicates to students that you don’t mean what you say. You’ve demonstrated that your expectations are mere suggestions and thus your words don’t matter.
Saying one thing and doing another is in the eyes of your students akin to lying. Hence, everything you say—including during your lessons—is called into question.
The solution is that everything you say must be backed by demonstrative action. You can never let anything go. It all matters.
But once you stand your ground, once you hold unyielding and honorable to the expectations and boundaries you know are best for your students, the tide will turn.
